content: Women who wish to initiate intrauterine contraception (IUC) during the postpartum period may benefit from having the device inserted immediately after delivery. Inserting the IUC postplacentally, within 10 minutes of placenta delivery, significantly reduces the risk of subsequent pregnancy and removes the need for a follow-up visit to begin contraception. Without the option of immediate insertion, many women may not return for contraceptive services or may resort to less effective methods. The objective of this study was to evaluate the outcomes of IUC insertion immediately after placenta delivery, particularly in comparison to insertion at other postpartum times. The primary outcomes assessed were successful placement of the IUC, rates of subsequent expulsion, and continued use of the method. To gather data, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including PubMed, CENTRAL, POPLINE, Web of Science, EMBASE, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, was conducted up to April 1, 2015. The authors also contacted investigators to identify additional trials. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with at least one treatment group involving immediate IUC placement (within 10 minutes of placenta delivery). Comparison groups could include early postpartum insertion (10 minutes postplacental to hospital discharge) or standard insertion (at a postpartum visit). Trials could also compare different IUC devices or insertion techniques, and deliveries could be vaginal or cesarean. The primary outcomes were IUC placement, expulsion rates, and method use at the time of study assessment. For dichotomous outcomes, the Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio (OR) with a 95% confidence interval (CI) was used. Earlier studies often reported results as life-table rates. Meta-analyses were performed when trials had similar interventions and outcome measures. Sensitivity analyses included studies with moderate or high-quality evidence and sufficient outcome data. Fifteen trials were included in the review. Seven studies published between 2010 and 2014 were added to eight from the original 2001 review. The newer trials compared immediate postplacental insertion with early insertion (10 minutes to 48 hours postpartum) or standard insertion (at a postpartum visit). Of the four newer trials with full reports, three were small, and the fourth was a pilot study. Three additional studies were only available as conference abstracts. The eight earlier trials, mostly from the 1980s, examined immediate insertion of various devices or techniques but often had limited reporting. The sensitivity analysis included trials with sufficient outcome data and moderate or high-quality evidence. Four newer trials comparing insertion times met the inclusion criteria. Two of these studies used the levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) after vaginal delivery, while the other two involved cesarean deliveries—one using the CuT 380A intrauterine device (IUD) and the other using the LNG-IUS. A pilot trial compared immediate insertion with early or standard insertion. In the group comparing immediate versus early insertion (N = 30), all participants received the LNG-IUS. By six months, the expulsion rates were the same between the groups, and there was no significant difference in IUC use. For immediate versus standard insertion, meta-analyses of four trials were conducted. The rates of successful insertion did not differ significantly between the groups. However, one trial from Uganda indicated that insertion was more likely in the immediate group, though the estimate was imprecise. In the meta-analysis, expulsion by six months was more likely in the immediate insertion group, but the confidence interval was wide (OR 4.89, 95% CI 1.47 to 16.32; participants = 210; studies = 4). IUC use at six months was more likely with immediate insertion compared to standard insertion (OR 2.04, 95% CI 1.01 to 4.09; participants = 243; studies = 4). However, in individual small trials, there was no significant difference in IUC use at three or twelve months between the groups. The authors concluded that recent trials comparing different insertion times after vaginal or cesarean delivery provided limited evidence due to small sample sizes in studies with full reports. The overall quality of evidence was moderate, with abstracts and older studies often lacking detailed reporting. Ongoing trials may contribute additional evidence, though some are also small in scale. Larger trials with adequate power are needed to better estimate expulsion rates and side effects. Despite the increased risk of expulsion, the benefit of effective contraception immediately after delivery may outweigh this disadvantage. Prenatal visits during the third trimester offer an opportunity to discuss effective contraceptive methods and the timing of initiation. Clinical follow-up is essential to detect early expulsion, and educating women about the signs and symptoms of expulsion can further support successful use of IUC.
